methodological_rigor.justification: The study employs appropriate statistical methodology for the comparison: linear regression with R2, Jonckheere-Terpstra test for ordered trends in ordinal-continuous associations, univariable and multivariable logistic regression for diagnostic associations, and bootstrap internal validation (2000 resamples) with optimism correction and calibration slope. The study avoids data-leakage by using a cohort independent of MelAInoma training data. The asymmetry in available data (MOLES with multimodal imaging vs. MelAInoma from single photograph) is clearly acknowledged as a limitation that would favor MOLES, making the MelAInoma result more noteworthy. The 5-year follow-up requirement for nevus classification strengthens ground truth reliability.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Distinguishing small choroidal melanomas from benign nevi is a clinically important and underserved problem in optometric triage, with direct implications for avoiding both delayed treatment of melanomas and unnecessary overtreatment of nevi. The finding that a single-photograph AI system performs comparably to expert multimodal MOLES scoring is highly practically relevant for primary care settings where OCT/autofluorescence are unavailable. The study directly addresses a real-world triage workflow problem with quantitative assessment.

reporting_quality.justification: The manuscript aligns well with STARD reporting requirements for diagnostic accuracy studies: patient population, eligibility criteria, reference standard, test execution, and performance statistics (AUC, OR, R2, calibration) are clearly described. Limitations including single-center design, absence of histopathologic confirmation, and shared-feature incorporation bias (MOLES/diagnosis overlap) are extensively discussed with balanced assessment. However, the dataset and algorithm code are not deposited publicly.

novelty_literature.justification: This is the first direct quantitative comparison of MOLES and MelAInoma in the same cohort using multivariable modeling to show independent additive value of each system. The finding that the two systems share only R2=0.16 variance and provide complementary information is an important practical insight for clinical implementation. The study extends prior work on each system individually but does not introduce a new diagnostic paradigm.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is exceptionally well written with careful discussion of the asymmetry between MOLES (multimodal, expert-applied) and MelAInoma (single photograph, algorithmic), which appropriately contextualizes the modest advantage of the AI. Limitations are enumerated in detail and analyzed for their directional impact. The statistical methods are described precisely and the bootstrap validation adds methodological rigor. The conclusion is appropriately tempered.

key_strengths: First head-to-head comparison of MOLES and MelAInoma in the same cohort with appropriate multivariable logistic regression showing independent additive information
Bootstrap internal validation with optimism correction (AUC 0.93→0.92) demonstrates model stability despite small sample
Thorough discussion of the informational asymmetry (MOLES had multimodal imaging; MelAInoma used only color photograph) that would favor MOLES, making AI performance more interpretable
key_concerns: Small cohort (n=86, 29 melanomas) limits statistical power and precision of the multivariable model; wide CIs on OR estimates reflect this
No histopathologic confirmation of diagnoses; clinical expert assessment as reference standard introduces shared-feature incorporation bias for MOLES
Single Swedish center limits generalizability to populations with different uveal melanoma incidence and referral patterns
External validation in independent multicenter cohorts is necessary before clinical deployment recommendations can be made
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically careful single-center study that provides clinically meaningful evidence for the complementary value of AI-based and manual triage systems for choroidal lesion assessment. The small sample, lack of histopathologic ground truth, and single-center design are acknowledged but limit generalizability. The work merits Tier 2 ophthalmic oncology consideration with minor revisions addressing external validation planning.
